Rider’s guide

How to read the card, ride your horse, and learn from the chart

You are the jockey. You choose one horse from the eight runners on the race card, then ride that horse through the race. You do not train, buy, or bet on the horses. Your decisions in the saddle determine how effectively you use the horse’s natural speed, stamina, running style, and quirks.

The central idea: your horse has a limited supply of energy. The goal is not to make her run as fast as possible at every moment. It is to save enough energy to finish the race strongly.

The day

Each day consists of five races, run in this order: Claiming, Allowance, Listed, Grade III, Grade I. The distance and surface are selected for each race. Races may be six or seven furlongs, one mile, nine furlongs, or ten furlongs, and may be run on dirt, turf, or synthetic. Only the two graded races may be run over ten furlongs; the other three are drawn from the shorter trips.

From the home page, choose Go to race card. Read the field, select a mount, and choose Start race. The field is led out onto the track in the post parade while the bugler plays the call to post, and then you are in the gate (click, or press Space, Enter or Esc, to skip the parade). After the race, the chart records the result and the day continues to the next race. Your record is saved in the browser, so you can close the game between races and resume later.

Reading the race card

The card gives you eight horses. The other riders are assigned after you choose your mount. Tap any horse to select it; you may change your selection until you start the race.

The most useful information on the card:

  • Program number: the horse’s saddlecloth number and starting stall. No. 1 is on the inside; No. 8 is on the outside.
  • Weight: the weight carried by the horse, including the rider’s allowance.
  • Medication: L means Lasix; b means blinkers.
  • Owner and trainer: part of the horse’s identity and the information tracked in the record book.
  • Breeding: sire, broodmare, and broodmare sire information.
  • Silks: the colors and pattern worn by the horse’s rider.
  • Morning line: the handicapper’s estimate of the horse’s relative chances, allowing for its running style, the draw and the trip. A short price is a real hint, but it is not a promise. The price a horse actually goes off at — its final odds — is set by the betting as the field loads, and is usually close to the line but never exactly on it.
  • Past performances: the link under each runner opens that horse’s form: one line for every start, most recent first, with the trip, the going, the fractions, where he lay at each call, the price and the caller’s note. The two figures are the track’s own — SF off the final time and PF off the half-mile, both against par for the trip. Ninety-two is a listed-class winner, and a class is worth about seven points. In the running line the small figure is the lengths he was behind the leader at that call — behind the winner at the finish — which is not how the chart counts them. Every line is a race actually run here. Races you have ridden are shaded; the oldest lines, dated before the meet opened, are from the pre-meet — four starts a horse, run the first time the game loads.
  • Running style: the most important tactical clue. A horse may be a front runner, stalker, or closer.

Controls

ControlWhat it does
↑ AskAsk the horse for more speed. A short tap gives a burst; holding it keeps the horse working harder and uses energy.
↓ HoldTake a hold and reduce the horse’s effort. This costs no energy and allows the horse to recover while traveling within herself.
← →Steer toward the rail or toward the outside. Running wide around a turn adds real distance. Hold the steer into a tight gap beside a horse to squeeze through it.
Enter CropUse the crop for a strong, brief surge. You have four uses for the race.
Space GogglesPull down a clean pair of goggles. You have four pairs. There is a brief moment when visibility is reduced while they are pulled down.
HShow the riding read-out: par and speed, energy, asking effort, resistance to the hold (labelled fight), path, ground lost, and reserve status.

Gamepad: right trigger or A to ask, left trigger or B to hold, stick or pad to steer, Y for the crop, X for goggles.

Touchscreen: the controls appear on the screen once you are loaded in the gate. Your left thumb steers with Rail and Out and has the goggles beside them. Your right thumb works Ask and Hold, and can slide from one to the other without lifting; the crop sits beside them. The marks under the crop and the goggles show how many uses you have left. Readout, at the top of the screen, does the same job as H, and Views hides or shows the two small camera views. On a phone the race is best ridden with the phone turned sideways.

The energy system

Every horse has one energy supply for the race. Speed uses that supply, and the cost rises sharply as you push the horse harder. A horse can recover while traveling within her normal effort, but there is no recovery during the final two furlongs. From that point to the finish, you must work with whatever energy remains.

The finishing reserve is especially important. Many horses have a stronger late effort that depends on saving energy earlier. Heavy asking before the halfway point can reduce that reserve permanently. In practical terms, two extra lengths early may cost you much more than two lengths late.

Use the H display. It lets you see whether your horse still has energy and whether her finishing reserve is intact. The audio is also useful: the horse’s breathing becomes louder and more labored as she tires.

Position, traffic, and the racing path

  • Buried: another horse is close in front and one is alongside. This is particularly uncomfortable for a front runner, somewhat costly for a stalker, and less troublesome for a closer.
  • Exposed: your horse is running in front with no horse to follow. This is hardest on a closer, which generally benefits from having horses to chase.
  • Kickback: on dirt, a horse behind another may receive dirt kicked back from the horse in front. Moving slightly off that horse’s path can reduce it.
  • Ground lost: running wide around a turn means traveling farther. Holding a horse toward the rail can save ground, but traffic and the horse’s own tendencies may make the inside difficult.
  • Squeezing through: hold the steer toward a gap — along the fence or between two horses — while a horse is beside or just ahead of you, and you ride him boot to boot instead of giving him a full path. It costs no energy. The risks: his rider may shut the door by coming over while he is still clear of you (frontrunners and horses that like the fence often do; horses that need room rarely can), and while your horse’s head is at his tail you can clip his heels — usually a stumble, sometimes a fall.

Riding by running style

TypeTypical approach
Front runnerWants to be near the lead and is uncomfortable behind other horses. Establish position early, preferably without spending more energy than necessary, then maintain a steady pace.
StalkerComfortable just behind the leaders. Try to stay close to the pace while saving energy, ideally with some cover from other horses. Look to improve position as the race turns for home.
CloserUsually wants to settle well behind the field and make one strong late run. Avoid spending energy early; the horse’s value comes from what she can do late.

Quirks matter. A horse that likes the fence is more comfortable inside traffic. A horse that needs room is more affected by being crowded. A puller resists a hold and takes longer to settle, so you may need to begin taking a hold earlier. A horse with turn of foot has an especially strong finishing reserve, making energy conservation even more important.

What you earn

RacePurseYour earnings for a win
Claiming$80,000$4,800
Allowance$100,000$6,000
Listed$200,000$12,000
Grade III$500,000$30,000
Grade I$1,000,000$60,000

The first five finishers are paid. The winner receives 60% of the purse and the fifth-place finisher receives 4%. Your earnings are 10% of whatever your horse wins. Because the purses increase substantially through the card, later races are worth much more than the early races.

The $2 win board

The home page ranks jockeys a second way: on what a $2 win ticket on every mount they rode would have returned, paid at the final odds. A winner at 8.40 to 1 returns $18.80; a loser returns nothing. The board shows the average return per $2 and the same figure as a gain or loss (ROI). A jockey needs 15 starts to be ranked.

The track keeps a cut of every pool, so a jockey whose horses win about as often as their odds say will average less than $2.00 — the typical rider sits around $1.45 (−27%). Finishing above $2.00 means bringing home more longshots than the betting expected. It is a statistic only: nothing is wagered, and it does not affect your earnings.

After the race

The results chart shows the entire field, the race fractions, final order, margins, and other details from the trip. Tap a runner to see that horse’s trip note. The Odds column gives each horse’s final odds (the favourite is marked *), and the $2 win payoff is printed under the final time. Your earnings are added to your record, and the jockey and horse standings and the $2 win board are updated.

Your record, the current day, and your place on the card are saved in the browser. Only races you actually ride count toward the record book.

Every race you ride also writes a line into the form book of all eight runners, so the horses you meet again on later cards carry the record of what they did under you. Your own name goes on those lines, on the card and in the standings; it is asked for once when you first open the game and can be changed from the home page.

A good way to learn. Start with a stalker. A stalker is generally the most forgiving running style because you do not need to establish the lead and you do not need to drop far out of the race. Use the H display, settle behind the leaders, and pay attention to your energy. Avoid spending heavily before the halfway point unless the situation clearly calls for it. As you approach the final turn, begin thinking about your position and how much energy you have saved for the finish.

Most important lesson: do not confuse activity with good riding. Asking, steering, and using the crop all have a purpose, but every unnecessary effort can leave your horse with less energy when it matters most.

The pre-meet

Before the first card, every horse on the grounds runs four races, so the form book is full of real races when you open it. They are being run now, by the same physics as the race you ride. This happens once.

Race 0

Your name, please

Every other rider in the room has one, and the chart wants a name in the brackets after the horse. Give yours once and the card, the chart, the form book and the standings will all carry it, set the way they set the rest of them.
